problems.description: Module-level global singleton `registry = ClientRegistry()` — global mutable state that tests must monkeypatch via the autouse fixture; fine at this scale but a mild smell that will complicate the Session 4 transport extraction.

ClientRegistry guards with `threading.Lock` inside a single-threaded asyncio server. All registry methods are synchronous (no awaits), so they are already atomic on the event loop; `asyncio.Lock` (or no lock) would be idiomatic. Harmless, but signals a concurrency-model mismatch.

The one measured convention hit inside this commit's diff: test_notification_server.py module-level constants flagged for UPPER_CASE (the other 5 violations land in app.py/conftest.py/test_redis_integration.py/transport.py, which are pre-existing scaffold files not added here).
No logging anywhere; broadcast/send_direct swallow ConnectionClosed silently, so production diagnostics for dropped connections would be difficult (consistent with the 2 SonarQube smells).

strengths: Faithful, complete implementation of the Session 1 greenfield spec: WebSocket server, unique client IDs, broadcast/direct/system message types, GET /health connected-client count, thread-safe registry, pytest + pytest-asyncio tests.
Clean layering (ClientRegistry, handle_message, handler, process_request) that anticipates Sessions 2-4: channels, Redis pub/sub, and pluggable transport extraction.

Zero bugs and zero duplications per SonarQube; +20 functions with single responsibilities and comprehensive tests covering fan-out, direct targeting, unique IDs, and error paths (invalid JSON, unsupported type, missing target).
Correct tech choices per spec: modern `websockets.asyncio.server` API rather than Flask-SocketIO, type hints on public signatures.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured, spec-faithful greenfield foundation with clean tests and zero bugs, whose only real blemishes are a global registry singleton, an unnecessary threading.Lock, and no logging — while the measured 0.82 convention score is dragged down mostly by pre-existing scaffold files (app.py, conftest.py, test_redis_integration.py, transport.py) that fall outside this commit's diff, a discrepancy worth flagging.

problems.description: subscribe/unsubscribe handlers are near-duplicates (~20 lines each: validation, error reply, registry call, ack reply); SonarQube +2 smells and +20 cognitive complexity corroborate. A shared validation/ack helper would halve the duplication.
ChannelRegistry.remove_client reimplements the 'discard and delete-if-empty' cleanup already present in unsubscribe; the empty-set eviction logic could be extracted.
No validation or length limit on channel names in subscribe; a client can subscribe to arbitrarily large/unique names, growing the _channels dict unboundedly.
remove_client iterates every channel on each disconnect (O(channels) per client); acceptable at current scale but could use a per-client inverse index if channel count grows.
The new http_get test helper parses and returns the status line but does not assert it; callers should assert HTTP 200 explicitly to catch regressions.

strengths: ChannelRegistry faithfully mirrors the established ClientRegistry pattern (lock-protected dict + the same method shapes), keeping thread safety conventions consistent.
Backwards compatible: broadcast without a 'channel' field still fans out to every connected client, so existing clients are unaffected.
Clean lifecycle handling — handler's finally block calls channels.remove_client, so subscriptions can't leak on disconnect.
The /channels and /channels/{name}/subscribers HTTP handlers follow the existing /health process_request pattern (Content-Type, sorted output).
Comprehensive async tests cover subscribe/unsubscribe acks, channel-routed broadcast, and the new HTTP endpoints.
CHANNEL_SUBSCRIBERS_PATH is a UPPER_CASE module-level compiled regex, and ChannelRegistry is PascalCase — the new code itself is convention-clean.
Uses registry.get(cid) with a None check in channel broadcast, correctly racing-safe against disconnects.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-integrated channel-subscription feature that follows the existing ClientRegistry and /health patterns with good tests and no bugs, only minor maintainability duplication and a slight rise in cognitive complexity.

problems.description: Race window: publish_event() fires immediately after ensure_started() spawns the worker, but redis_worker subscribes asynchronously — a message published before the subscription completes is silently dropped, and no redelivery mechanism exists.

Cognitive complexity +36 is a large one-commit increase, concentrated in the lazy-init/worker lifecycle (ensure_started, redis_worker, deliver_broadcast) plus the new Redis+SQLite dual-persistence paths.

Duplications +5.7%: the connection.send(...) / except ConnectionClosed: pass / connection-is-None guard pattern is duplicated across deliver_broadcast and deliver_direct instead of being extracted into one send helper.
store_message() opens a fresh aiosqlite connection per message rather than reusing a shared connection/pool; fine at low volume but wasteful at broadcast scale.

Module-level mutable globals (redis_client, _worker_task, _db_ready) with lock-guarded mutation add hidden state; it does mirror the existing module-level registry pattern, but triples the count of such globals.

Static analysis flags conftest.py for PascalCase-class and UPPER_CASE-constant violations, but the shown file contains no class and no module-level constant — the rule appears misattributed. The other flagged files (app.py, transport.py, tests) are not part of this diff, so the commit's attributable convention load is lower than the 0.82 aggregate suggests.

strengths: Autouse fakeredis + tmp SQLite fixture gives every test full isolation without requiring a real redis-server, a genuine CI/testability win.

Clean separation of publish (publish_event) from delivery (deliver_broadcast/deliver_direct), where delivery only touches local registries — this correctly enables multiple instances to share the Redis backbone.
Idempotent, lock-guarded lazy startup (ensure_started) makes it safe to call from any request handler, matching the module's existing lazy/mutable-state style.
Docstrings clearly document the multi-instance delivery semantics and the connected-client mirroring rationale.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-argued Session 3 integration that adds a Redis pub/sub backbone and SQLite history to the notification server with excellent test isolation, but it lands a large complexity jump, a subscribe/publish race that can drop messages, and some duplicated delivery code.

problems.description: Abstract method signatures use *args/**kwargs (on_connect, send_message, broadcast), which weakens the transport contract: the ABC no longer enforces a fixed signature, so implementations and callers lose static-checking guarantees.
on_connect() returning a newly generated client_id moves client-ID ownership into the transport; generating IDs is a routing concern and may duplicate/conflict with ID logic in the server core.

transport.py is flagged for a module-level constant casing violation per static analysis, though the diff shown contains no module-level constants — likely a false positive or referring to the full-file variant (type-alias assignments).
The commit delivers only the interface with no concrete implementation, so the abstraction is unexercised and untested until a concrete transport is wired in.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: wire-protocol specifics (connection tracking, delivery) are isolated behind an interface; core logic never touches a connection object directly.
Well-documented design intent in the module docstring, making the extensibility story (SSE, long-polling, raw TCP) explicit.
Correct ABC/abstractmethod usage with snake_case methods and fully-typed message payloads (str).
SonarQube clean: no new bugs, smells, or cognitive complexity, and duplications actually dropped 0.1%.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound dependency-inversion refactor that cleanly abstracts the wire protocol behind a documented BaseTransport interface, held back only by loose *args/**kwargs signatures and an interface-without-implementation step.

compounding_issues: Session 1 discarded the Flask Todo seed entirely (greenfield rewrite), so the seed's seams provided no reuse value — acceptable for a greenfield session but the seed effort was wasted
Session 3 opened the SQLite connection in __init__ and does synchronous blocking writes (store_message/commit) inside async paths, a latency coupling that persisted into later sessions
Session 3's Redis integration silently degrades to single-server mode when Redis is unreachable (try/except swallows the failure), which can mask misconfiguration in production

Session 4's transport refactor left two source-of-truth registries — WebSocketTransport._connections and NotificationServer.clients — that must be kept in sync via dual on_connect/on_disconnect handlers, a mild redundancy
key_decisions: Session 1: Greenfield async WebSocket server (NotificationServer) built from scratch over an async/threading split (asyncio event loop + RLock-protected client registry), replacing the seed
Session 2: Channel subscription model (subscribe/unsubscribe message types, per-client channel registry, HTTP channel listing) making routing data-driven rather than hardcoded broadcast
Session 3: Redis pub/sub for cross-server message fan-out with SQLite persistence for message history — introduced multi-instance distribution and durable store with an optional, guarded dependency
Session 4: Transport abstraction (BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport) decoupling server logic from the websockets library, enabling future alternate transports
Session 5: Cross-cutting operational hardening — Redis-backed rate limiting with local fallback, message TTL cleanup loop, and a paginated /history endpoint reusing the Session 3 persistence layer
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions and stayed green at every checkpoint. Session 1 established a clean single-file async server with a solid 5-test suite; Session 2 added channels cleanly with tests; Session 3 layered Redis pub/sub and SQLite persistence, materially raising architectural ambition while keeping tests green. Session 4 was a well-executed refactor that extracted the transport layer — the most consequential structural change — and Session 5 built on every prior layer (rate limiting via the transport seam, history via the SQLite store, cleanup independent of Redis) rather than bolting on parallel machinery. The final state is 442 lines of server plus a 101-line transport module with all 10 tests passing, showing disciplined incremental composition where each session's additions were surgical and consistent with prior decisions.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, steadily-improving progression from greenfield async server through channels, Redis/SQLite integration, transport refactor, and cross-cutting operational features, with only minor accrued debt (blocking SQLite writes in async paths and a duplicated connection registry) that never compromised correctness.
